terms.plain: The basic body measurements that show how a person is doing right now. They are temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, and often pain and oxygen level.
terms.matters: Vital signs are how a care team spots trouble early. You take them, so you are often the first to see a change.

terms.plain: The force of blood pushing against the walls of the arteries. It is written as two numbers, like 122/78.
terms.matters: The two numbers tell the care team how hard the heart is working and how open the blood vessels are.

terms.plain: The top number. It is the pressure in the arteries at the moment the heart squeezes and pushes blood out.
terms.matters: You find it by listening for the very first clear tapping sound as the cuff lets go.

terms.plain: The bottom number. It is the pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats.
terms.matters: You find it at the point where the tapping sounds stop and silence returns.

terms.plain: The unit blood pressure is measured in. It stands for millimeters of mercury. A reading of 122 means 122 mmHg.
terms.matters: Old gauges used a tube of mercury. The unit stayed even though the mercury did not.

terms.plain: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to the rest of the body.
The main artery of the upper arm. You can feel it on the inner side of the elbow, closer to the body than the center.
terms.matters: The cuff squeezes this artery and the stethoscope listens to it. Miss the spot and you miss the sounds.

terms.plain: The pulse you feel at the thumb side of the wrist.
terms.matters: Feeling this pulse while you inflate gives you a rough guess of the top number before you listen.

terms.plain: To feel something with your fingertips on purpose, such as finding a pulse or a landmark on the body.
Listening to sounds inside the body with a stethoscope.
terms.matters: A manual blood pressure is an auscultatory measurement. Your ears are the instrument.

terms.plain: The tapping and whooshing sounds you hear through the stethoscope while the cuff lets go. They are made by blood pushing through an artery that is still partly squeezed.
terms.matters: The first sound marks the top number. The last sound marks the bottom number. Everything else is the road between them.

terms.plain: The full name for a blood pressure cuff set: the cuff, the tubing, the bulb with its valve, and the gauge.
The round dial with a needle that shows the pressure in the cuff. It has no liquid inside.
terms.matters: Your eyes stay on this dial while your ears follow the sounds. Reading it is half the skill.

terms.plain: Checking that the needle rests exactly on zero when no air is in the cuff.
terms.matters: A gauge that sits 4 mmHg high at rest is 4 mmHg wrong at every reading you take with it. Check it before you trust it.

terms.plain: The wide band that wraps around the arm and squeezes it when you pump air in.
The balloon inside the cuff that fills with air. It is smaller than the cloth cover around it.
terms.matters: Cuff size rules are really bladder rules. The cloth may reach around an arm the bladder is far too small for.

terms.plain: The small screw on the bulb that lets air out. Turning it clockwise closes it. Turning it counterclockwise opens it a little at a time.
terms.matters: The valve is where the whole skill lives. A steady hand here is what makes a reading trustworthy.

terms.plain: The listening tool. Earpieces go in your ears, and the flat round end goes on the skin over the artery.
The flat, round side of the stethoscope head. It picks up higher sounds, which is what blood pressure sounds are.
terms.matters: The cup-shaped side, called the bell, is for lower sounds. Use the flat side for blood pressure unless your program says otherwise.

terms.plain: To close something off so nothing can pass through.
terms.matters: When the cuff is above the top number, it occludes the artery. No blood passes, so there is no sound.

terms.plain: To pump air into the cuff so it tightens around the arm.
How fast you let air out of the cuff, measured in mmHg per second. The rate you are learning is 2 to 3 mmHg per second, which is about one small mark on the dial each second.
terms.matters: Let air out too fast and the sounds fly past your ears, so both numbers come out low. Too slow and the arm aches and the numbers drift.

terms.plain: The bend on the inner side of the elbow.
terms.matters: The bottom edge of the cuff goes 2 to 3 cm above this crease — about 1 inch — so the cuff does not sit on top of your stethoscope.

terms.plain: The distance all the way around the upper arm, measured at the middle, between the shoulder and the elbow.
terms.matters: This one number decides your cuff. Measure it instead of guessing by eye.

terms.plain: The height of the middle of the chest, about the fourth rib. The cuffed arm should be supported at this height.
terms.matters: An arm held below heart level reads high. An arm held above it reads low. Gravity does not care how well you listen.

terms.plain: A person's overall body build and size.
terms.matters: Body build changes which cuff fits, and cuff fit changes the reading.

terms.plain: Relating to the care of people with obesity. A bariatric cuff is an extra-large cuff.
Relating to the care of children.
terms.matters: Children need child-sized cuffs, and normal values for children are not the adult 120/80.

terms.plain: A newborn baby in the first month of life.
A way of comparing one child to other children of the same age, sex, and height. A blood pressure at the 90th percentile is higher than 90 out of 100 similar children.
terms.matters: Child blood pressure is judged against percentiles, not against one fixed number.

terms.plain: Blood pressure that stays higher than normal over time.
terms.matters: One high reading is not hypertension. It takes repeated readings, and a licensed provider makes the call.

terms.plain: Blood pressure that is lower than normal.
terms.matters: A low reading in a person who looks unwell is urgent. Report it right away.

terms.plain: A blood pressure high enough to need attention right now, usually 180 or higher on top, or 120 or higher on the bottom.
terms.matters: This is a stop-what-you-are-doing number. Stay with the person and get the nurse.

terms.plain: What is usual for one person. It is found by looking at their past readings in the chart.
terms.matters: A reading of 148 may be routine for one resident and an emergency for another. Compare to the person, not just the textbook.

terms.plain: A rise in blood pressure caused by nerves around medical staff and medical places.
terms.matters: A calm greeting and a few quiet minutes are not just good manners. They protect the number.

terms.plain: A stretch of silence in the middle of the sounds. The tapping starts, disappears for a while, then comes back.
terms.matters: If you start listening inside the gap, you will record a top number that is far too low. Pumping up 30 above your felt guess protects you from this.

terms.plain: A heartbeat that is uneven or irregular.
terms.matters: When beats are uneven, each beat gives a slightly different pressure. Take the reading, note what you heard, and tell the nurse.

terms.plain: A reason not to do something to a certain person or a certain body part.
terms.matters: Some arms must never be used for a blood pressure. Checking first takes seconds and prevents real harm.

terms.plain: A surgically made connection between an artery and a vein in the arm, used for dialysis.
terms.matters: Never put a cuff on this arm. Squeezing it can damage the access the person depends on.

terms.plain: Surgery to remove a breast. It sometimes includes removing lymph nodes in the armpit.
terms.matters: Use the other arm when nodes were removed on that side, unless the care plan says otherwise.

terms.plain: Swelling caused by extra fluid in the tissue. Pressing it may leave a dent.
terms.matters: A swollen arm gives an unreliable reading and can be painful under a cuff. Use the other arm and report it.

terms.plain: A thin tube placed in a vein to give fluids or medicine.
terms.matters: A cuff over an IV can stop the flow or push fluid into the tissue. Use the other arm.

terms.plain: Cleaning your hands with soap and water or with hand sanitizer.
terms.matters: It is the single strongest step you take to keep infection from moving between residents.

terms.plain: Two separate ways of confirming who a person is, such as their full name and their date of birth.
terms.matters: A perfect reading recorded in the wrong chart is worse than no reading at all.

terms.plain: A reading that comes out higher than the person's real blood pressure because of a mistake in how it was taken.
terms.matters: A cuff that is too small, an unsupported arm, or no rest period all push the number up.

terms.plain: A reading that comes out lower than the person's real blood pressure because of a mistake in how it was taken.
terms.matters: A cuff that is too large, letting air out too fast, or starting below a silent gap all pull the number down.

terms.plain: The habit of rounding readings to numbers that end in 0 or 5 without meaning to.
terms.matters: Real blood pressures do not favor zeros. If most of your readings end in 0, your eyes are rounding for you.

terms.plain: The set of tasks you are trained, allowed, and expected to do in your role.
terms.matters: Measuring and reporting are yours. Diagnosing and changing medicine are not. Knowing the line keeps everyone safe.

terms.plain: A registered nurse (RN) or licensed practical nurse (LPN). They are the supervisor you report your readings to.
terms.also_called: RN or LPN, the charge nurse

terms.plain: To pass information up to someone with more authority, right away, so they can act on it.
terms.matters: Escalating is not admitting you failed. It is the step the whole system depends on you taking.

terms.plain: The written record of what you did and what you found, entered in the chart.
terms.matters: If you did not document it, then legally it did not happen.

terms.plain: Pediatric Advanced Life Support. It is the standard set of rules for caring for a very sick child.
terms.matters: PALS sets the low blood pressure limits that mean a child needs help right now.

terms.plain: A person who lives in a long-term care home. In a hospital the same person would be called a patient.
